newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FDA backs Hologic bone mineral device.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FDA backs Hologic bone mineral device.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration advisory panel on Monday voted unanimously to approve, with conditions, Hologic Inc.'s Sahara ultrasound device, used to estimate bone mineral density.

Bone mineral density (BMD) strongly predicts the risk for osteoporosis, estimated to affect at least 23 million American, primarily white, women. Osteoporosis costs the country $14 billion a year, which includes drug therapies and hospitalization for fractures.
The panel said that Hologic needs to include more information in its labeling on usage by men and non-white females, and better physician and patient education about when to use the device.
The FDA is not bound by its panels' advice, but usually follows it.

Hologic said that Sahara is as clinically useful and cheaper, safer and more accessible than dual X-ray absorptionetry (DXA). But the panel said that Sahara can only be used to "predict" results of DXA, which may curb enthusiasm for the device.
Hologic has said that Sahara, a $30,000, 20-pound device, may increase access to screening and therefore treatment.

An estimated 70 percent of women with osteoporosis are undiagnosed. But screening is only currently recommended for women known to be at high risk -- those who are small boned, thin, post-menopausal, or with family history.

DXA requires a large X-ray unit that uses ionizing radiation, and directly measures BMD. Sahara uses harmless ultrasound to estimate BMD. With Sahara, a patient simply places her foot in the machine, and a measurement is taken in about a minute, compared to ten minutes for DXA.

Despite its safety, panelists had some concern that using Sahara, doctors might miss some patients who needed drug therapy. That's because the FDA said that Hologic's study data showed that women's T-scores -- a measure of disease -- with Sahara could differ by two or more points from DXA. That could be confusing for clinicians, FDA said.

Hologic said that in a trial in 247 women -- all Caucasian -- comparing DXA and Sahara, the results were highly correlated at a rate of 0.85. The rate is similar to that seen when other bone density technologies are compared, and clinically acceptable, said Hologic.

Richard Mazess, president of Hologic's chief competitor, Lunar Corp., said at the panel hearing morning that DXA and Sahara were not "highly" correlated. Hologic president Jay Stein countered that Mazess' comments should be tempered by the fact that Sahara would "compete very directly and very heavily" with Lunar's DXA system.
Panelists said results of the two systems were "correlated," but did not say that they were "highly correlated."
Hologic closed at 21-5/8 on Friday, and was up more than $1 in heavy trading after the panel decision on Monday.
